issues.item: Compulsive Exercise: I push myself to exercise excessively
issues.explanation: Compulsive exercise is weakly integrated with the rest of the profile. The other selected items cluster around hypervigilance, dissociation, memory disorganisation, and danger-based appraisals after terrorism. Excessive exercise does not clearly serve or connect to those symptoms, making it look like a strategy for a different presentation unless additional context were present.

issues.item: Life Not Worth Living: I am not sure my life is worth living anymore
issues.explanation: 'Life Not Worth Living' is disproportionately severe relative to the rest of the selected profile and is not well supported by the surrounding appraisals. The other appraisals focus on danger and bodily unreliability, while the threat/memory items emphasize hyperarousal and fragmented recall. This suicidal-hopelessness appraisal can occur in PTSD, but here it stands out as insufficiently linked to the rest of the formulation and item set.

vignette: Anaís Hernández's eyes would often glaze over as she recounted the night of the terrorist bombing at the concert venue where she had been celebrating her 28th birthday with friends. It was a year ago, but the memory still felt like an open wound. She remembered the sound of shattering glass, the screams, and the feeling of being trampled in the stampede to escape. But there were gaps in her recollection, moments that refused to resurface no matter how hard she tried. When fragments did come back to her, they were often accompanied by a rage so intense it left her breathless. She would get angry at herself for not being able to recall every detail, feeling like she was somehow responsible for the attack. Anaís's mind kept replaying the image of a broken exit sign and a sea of panicked faces, which seemed to be seared into her memory forever. As a warehouse manager in a predominantly male-dominated field, Anaís used to take pride in her ability to stay composed under pressure. However, in the months following the attack, she found herself becoming increasingly withdrawn. She avoided social gatherings and stopped attending concerts or festivals, fearing that another attack could happen at any moment. At work, she would constantly scan her surroundings, checking for potential threats – a suspicious package, an unattended bag, or a stranger lingering in the warehouse's corridors. Her coworkers began to notice her jitters, how she would startle at the slightest noise, and how she seemed to be always "on edge." Anaís couldn't explain why; all she knew was that she felt safer when she was aware of her environment. She started carrying a small flashlight with her at all times, which she would use to scan dark corners or under shelves whenever she felt anxious. Anaís's hypervigilance seeped into other areas of her life as well. At night, Anaís would lie awake for hours, listening for any unusual sounds outside her apartment in the predominantly Latinx neighborhood where she grew up. Her mind was a constant battlefield, with thoughts racing through her head like warning sirens blaring in the night. She would ruminate on what-ifs and maybes, wondering if there were signs she had missed that could have prevented the attack. What frightened her most was the thought of losing control again, of being trapped in a situation where she couldn't escape. When interacting with others, Anaís would deliberately avoid eye contact, fearing that she might see something in their gaze that would trigger another flashback or panic attack. In crowded spaces, she felt the urge to dissociate, to leave her body behind and observe the scene from afar – anything to escape the overwhelming sense of vulnerability. Anaís's relationships began to suffer as well. Friends would invite her out, only to be met with hesitation or last-minute cancellations. Her family grew concerned about her increasing isolation and tried to intervene, but Anaís pushed them away, convinced that they couldn't understand what she was going through. She felt like she was living in a state of perpetual limbo, unable to shake the feeling that something was off, even when everything seemed fine on the surface. The warehouse job, once a source of comfort and routine, now felt like a potential trap – another site where disaster could strike at any moment. Anaís found herself questioning her own memory and perception, wondering if she had imagined certain details or exaggerated others. She started to doubt her ability to make decisions, fearing that she might misread situations or overlook crucial information. It wasn't until a particularly harrowing night, when Anaís found herself unable to shake the image of a stranger lurking outside her apartment window, that she realized she needed help. She began to wonder if there was more to life than just surviving from one day to the next. As she finally reached out for therapy, Anaís couldn't shake off the feeling that seeking help would somehow make her vulnerable all over again – but it was a risk she was willing to take, desperate to rediscover some semblance of peace and trust in herself and the world around her. With a mix of trepidation and hope, Anaís took the first step towards healing, unsure of what lay ahead but determined to reclaim her life from the grip of fear and uncertainty.
